parole.significato: house, home (structure built or serving as an abode of human beings)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek σπίτιν (spítin), from earlier or Koine Greek ὁσπίτιον (hospítion), from Latin hospitium (“lodgings”). Compare Albanian shtëpi and Sicilian spizziu. Displaced earlier Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos).

parole.significato: stable (a building, wing or dependency set apart and adapted for lodging and feeding ungulates)
parole.testo: Inherited from Koine Greek στάβλος m (stáblos), from στάβλον n (stáblon), from Latin stabulum.
From Byzantine Greek κιστέρνα (kistérna, “cistern”), from Latin cisterna (“cistern”), from Latin cista, from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē).

parole.significato: tern (a bird of the family Sternidae)
parole.testo: From New Latin sternidae (“tern family of birds”).
Borrowed from Latin strata. Compare Italian strada.

Inherited from Byzantine Greek στρίγκλα (strínkla), from Latin strigula, diminutive of striga, from the στριγγ- stem of Koine Greek στρίγξ (strínx) (whence also Latin strīx), from Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx).

parole.significato: board (committee that manages the business of an organization)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συμβούλιον (sumboúlion, “advice, counsel”), a Hellenistic semantic loan from Latin consilium. For sense "managing board", a free translation or semantic loan for the French conseil.

parole.significato: soda, soda water, club soda (carbonated water)
parole.testo: From New Latin soda, from Arabic سُوَّد (suwwad, “saltwort”).

Learned borrowing from Koine Greek σῠ́γκλητος (sŭ́nklētos), from the ancient adjective σῠ́γκλητος (sŭ́nklētos), from Ancient Greek σῠγκᾰλέω (sŭnkăléō, “to call to council, convoke, convene”), συγ- (syg-, “with, together”) + κλητός (klitós, “called”), equivalent to συν- (syn-) + καλώ (kaló, “to call,
Inherited from Byzantine Greek τάβλι (tábli, a game with dice). Ultimately, from Koine Greek τάβλα (tábla), from Latin tabula.
Borrowed from Latin taberna (“inn, tavern, shop”).
Learnedly formed from the τελεσι- stem of Ancient Greek τέλος (télos) and -γραφον, neuter singular of -γραφος (-graphos). A loose calque of Latin ultimātum.
Substantivized passive perfect participle of τέμνω (témno, “to cut”). Its use in modern mathematical geometry is as a semantic loan from Latin abscissa.
From τετραγωνίζω (tetragonízo, “to square”) + -ίστρια (-ístria, feminine agent noun), a calque of New Latin quadratrix.
Learned borrowing from New Latin telescopium, from Ancient Greek τηλεσκόπος (tēleskópos, “far-seeing”) + -ιον (-ion), from τηλε- (tēle-, “far”) + σκοπέω, σκοπῶ (skopéō, skopô, “to look”).

parole.significato: brick (hardened rectangular block of mud, clay etc., used for building)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek τοῦβλον (toûblon), from Koine Greek τούβουλον (toúboulon), from Latin tubulus (“small tube”).
Reborrowing from Latin tumba (“small mound”), from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos, “small mound”)

parole.significato: cake with layers of filling and icing, similar to birthday or wedding cakes
parole.testo: Inherited from Ancient Greek τούρτα (“kind of baked bread”), from Latin turta, perhaps ultimately from Latin tŏrta (“twisted”). The association with a "round cake" is an influence by the Italian torta.
From τριβο- (trivo-, “tribo-”) + χημεία (chimeía, “chemistry; from Late Latin chēmia, from Ancient Greek χυμεία (khumeía, “art of alloying metals”).”)
Borrowed from New Latin trichiurus, from Ancient Greek θρίξ (thríx, “hair”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).
From Byzantine Greek τροῦλλος (troûllos), a borrowing from Latin trulla. Cognate with Greek τούρλα (toúrla).

From Byzantine Greek τσεκούριον (tsekoúrion, “axe”), from Koine Greek σεκούριον (sekoúrion, “axe”), from Latin securis (“axe”). Compare Romanian secure and more distantly Serbo-Croatian сѐкира, Bulgarian секи́ра (sekíra).
Hellenised form of New Latin typographia
Inherited from Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos). The mathematical sense, a semantic loan from New Latin locus.

parole.significato: postscript, PS (footnote or addendum in correspondence)
parole.testo: From υστερό- (ysteró-, “after, subsequent”) + γραφή (grafí, “writing”), a calque of New Latin postscriptum. First attested 1840.
From φασκιώνω (faskióno, “to swaddle”), from Koine Greek φασκιῶ (phaskiô), from Koine Greek φασκία (phaskía), from Latin fascia (“strip, ribbon”).
From Koine Greek φασκία (phaskía), from Latin fascia (“strip, ribbon”).
From Byzantine Greek φασκιώνω (phaskiṓnō), from Koine Greek φασκιῶ (phaskiô) + -ώνω (suffix for verbs), from φασκία (phaskía), from Latin fascia (“strip, ribbon”).

Inherited from Byzantine Greek φασόλιν (phasólin) < *φασιόλιον, from diminutive of Hellenistic Koine Greek φασίολος (phasíolos), a reborrowing from Latin phaseolus, diminutive of phaselus, from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos) a bean probably of the Vigna genus. Also see φασούλι.
Calque of Medieval Latin circulus vitiōsus.
From φούρναρ(ης) (foúrnar(is), “baker”, masculine) + -ισσα (-issa, femminine suffix). See φούρνος (foúrnos, “oven”), from Latin furnus.

parole.significato: tuft, a bunch of yarns joined at only one end
parole.testo: From Koine Greek φοῦνδα (phoûnda), from Latin funda (“slingshot”).
Stress shift from Byzantine Greek φουρνάρης (phournárēs), derived from Late Latin furnārius.
From Ancient Greek φοῦρνος (phoûrnos), from Latin furnus (“oven, bakery”).
From Byzantine Greek φράγουλα (phrágoula), from Vulgar Latin *frāgula.
Borrowed from Latin fructus.

parole.significato: for, as (equivalent to the Latin gratia)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χάριν (khárin), accusative singular form of χάρις (kháris, “grace”) used adverbially. For sense "as", semantic loan from New Latin gratia. Also see χάρις (cháris) & χάρη f (chári, “favour, grace”).
From Late Latin chēmia, from Ancient Greek χυμεία (khumeía, “art of alloying metals”).
From Latin humus (“soil, earth”).
Borrowed from New Latin osmium.
